opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really good principle, and honestly it's one that I think most of us building frameworks end up converging on, whether or not we name it that way. François articulated it very cleanly with Keras: you should be able to get started with something very simple, like a `model.fit`, and then as your needs grow, you peel back a layer and write your own training loop, and then another layer, and you're writing your own layers, your own gradients, and so on. You never hit a wall where you suddenly have to throw everything away and start over in a completely different system.

Where I'd add some nuance is that the principle sounds simple, but the hard part is deciding *where* the layers are and what the "default" level should be. With PyTorch, our bet was a bit different in emphasis. We assumed our core users were researchers who were going to want to be close to the metal pretty much from day one. So instead of starting at a very high-level abstraction and letting you dig down, we tried to make the lower level itself feel simple: it's just Python, it's just tensors, you write a for loop, you call backward, you step the optimizer. The idea was that if the "complex" layer is actually pleasant and debuggable, you don't need as many layers on top of it. And then the community built the higher-level stuff on top: things like Lightning, fastai, Hugging Face's Trainer, and so on.

So in some sense it's the same philosophy approached from opposite directions. Keras started high and progressively exposed what's underneath. PyTorch started low and let the ecosystem progressively hide complexity for people who wanted that. Both are trying to avoid the cliff, that moment where the abstraction breaks and you're stuck.

The other thing I'd say is that every abstraction you add is a promise you have to keep. When you expose a layer of complexity, people build on it, and now you can't change it easily. So I'm always a little cautious about adding abstraction layers just for elegance. I'd rather have fewer layers that are each really solid and transparent than many layers that leak. But as a guiding principle for usability, that you shouldn't have to pay the complexity cost until you actually need the power, I think François is absolutely right, and it's a big part of why Keras was so successful at bringing people into deep learning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think François is right about the principle, and I also think it's one of those principles that sounds obviously correct until you actually try to build it, and then it turns out to be genuinely hard.

The idea, as I understand it, is that a user should be able to start at the top of a stack with something very simple, like `model.fit`, and then only when they need more control do they peel back a layer, and then another layer, and at each step the thing they learn on the layer above is still useful on the layer below. You never have a cliff where you go from "this is magic" to "now rewrite everything in a completely different mental model." Keras did a really nice job of that, especially the arc from Sequential to the functional API to subclassing. That's a very deliberate design, and I have a lot of respect for it.

Where PyTorch came from was a slightly different place. We started basically at the bottom. The original bet was: give people tensors, give them autograd, give them Python, and get out of the way. So in a sense we exposed almost all the complexity on day one, and the only thing that saved us was that the complexity was in Python, where people already knew how to manage it. Researchers didn't want a framework to hide things from them, they wanted a framework that didn't surprise them. The "progressive" part came later, and honestly it came from the community more than from us. Things like Lightning, fastai, Hugging Face's Trainer, those are the high-level layers that give you the simple on-ramp, and underneath they're just normal PyTorch, so when you hit a wall you can drop down and nothing changes about how you think.

So I'd say the two philosophies converge on the same destination but from opposite directions. Keras designed the layers top-down and then had to make sure the bottom was expressive enough. We built the bottom and then let an ecosystem grow the layers on top. There are tradeoffs. The Keras approach gives you more coherence, the ecosystem approach gives you more diversity and sometimes fragmentation, and you have to be okay with the fact that there are five ways to write a training loop.

The thing I'd add, and where I'd push on the principle a bit, is that "complexity" isn't one axis. There's conceptual complexity, like do I understand what a layer is, and then there's performance complexity, like do I understand why this is slow, or why it's using this much memory, or what's happening on the device. And the second kind is much harder to expose progressively, because the abstractions that make the first kind easy actively hide the second kind. A lot of the pain in deep learning frameworks over the last few years, including ours, has been about that: how do you keep the eager, hackable, debuggable experience while also letting someone say "now make this fast" without forcing them to learn a compiler. torch.compile is basically our attempt at applying François's principle to performance rather than to modeling. You write the simple thing, and you opt in to the next layer when you need it.

So, short version: I agree with the principle, I think Keras executed it better than anyone on the modeling side, and I think the frontier now is applying it to the parts of the stack that are much less forgiving.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a good principle. You want someone to get started without having to understand every detail, and then expose more as they need it. The difficult question is what happens when they want to do something that your abstraction didn’t anticipate.

In a deep learning framework, that happens pretty quickly, especially in research. You might start with a standard training loop, but then you want to change how gradients are computed or update different parts of the model at different times. If getting there requires abandoning the high-level API and learning a completely different system, then the complexity hasn’t really been exposed progressively. There’s a cliff.

So I agree with the principle. With PyTorch, the emphasis is on making the underlying pieces understandable and composable, so that moving beyond the simple case feels like extending the code you already have. There’s a tradeoff: you might write a little more code initially, but you have more room to change what that code does.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a good principle. You want someone to get started without having to understand every detail of the system. But the question is what happens when they want to do something that the high-level interface didn’t anticipate. Can they go one level deeper and still understand what’s going on, or do they suddenly have to understand the entire framework?

For me, that transition is really important. A simple interface is useful, but you also want the underlying pieces to be accessible and composable. You should be able to change the training loop, inspect a tensor, or write a new operation without feeling like you’ve stepped into a completely different world. So I agree with progressively exposing complexity; I’d put a lot of emphasis on making that progression feel continuous.
